title: A House Divided, Written Down
subtitle: The American Civil War: Fort Sumter, Emancipation Day, Gettysburg and Vicksburg, Columbia, and Lincoln's death
intro: Four years, three quarters of a million dead, and four million people freed from slavery: the American Civil War was fought by a highly literate population that wrote constantly. Soldiers carried pocket diaries, planters' daughters kept journals under their beds, and cabinet secretaries wrote at midnight. Rarely has a war been recorded so densely from so many sides at once.

This chapter gathers those records at five moments. At Fort Sumter in April 1861 the war began, watched from a Charleston rooftop and read about under the lamps of Broadway. On 1 January 1863 the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, and at Camp Saxton in South Carolina formerly enslaved soldiers, a free Black teacher and an abolitionist colonel recorded the same ceremony from yards apart. In July 1863 came Gettysburg and Vicksburg, seen by a British guardsman up a tree, a Rhode Island lieutenant in the line, a poet in the hospitals and the clerks of two capitals. On 17 February 1865 Columbia burned around a seventeen-year-old diarist, and on 14–15 April 1865 Lincoln died, with the Navy Secretary at the bedside and the news then spreading across the country.

The eyes do not agree, and that is the point. Chesnut and Stone write the Confederacy's grief and, in Stone's case, open joy at Lincoln's death. Forten and Taylor record freedom as something lived, not granted. Fremantle came as an admiring foreign visitor and saw a defeat he did not fully grasp. Handy, a hostile witness, preserves the scale of a Black celebration that the law said should not have happened.

Honesty about form matters here more than in most wars, because many famous 'diaries' were rewritten. Chesnut reworked hers in the 1880s, Whitman built Specimen Days from notebooks two decades later, and Susie King Taylor wrote her memoir in 1902. These are flagged and kept, because without them the Black and Confederate women's voices would thin out. Wherever a date or detail could not be re-verified for this edition, the entry is marked approximate.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian, the civil calendar of the United States throughout. Several key entries were written the morning after the night they describe (LeConte on Columbia, Welles on Lincoln's death), so the book places them on the night's date and notes when they were written.

eyes.name: Mary Boykin Chesnut
eyes.role: 38-year-old wife of ex-Senator James Chesnut Jr., aide to Beauregard; planter-class hostess
eyes.where: Mills House hotel, Charleston, April 1861; later Columbia, Chester and Lincolnton NC
eyes.vantage_label: on the housetop, wife of an envoy
eyes.authenticity: REVISED. She kept journals 1861–65, then rewrote them in the 1880s as a literary work in diary form. Editions of 1905 and 1949 used the revision; C. Vann Woodward's 'Mary Chesnut's Civil War' (1981, Pulitzer) prints the 1880s text, and 'The Private Mary Chesnut' (1984) prints the surviving original journals, which cover 1861 and parts of 1862 and 1865. Read her as a later shaping of real notes.
eyes.bio: The most famous Confederate diarist: sharp, gossipy, at dinner tables where secession was decided. Her husband personally carried the ultimatum to Fort Sumter, so she spent the bombardment's first hours in the inner circle, yet she also kept looking at the enslaved people around her and wondering what they really thought.

sources.title: American Battlefield Trust: excerpt, April 1861
NPS biography
Emerging Civil War: 'And So We Took Fort Sumter' (cites Woodward 1981)

eyes.name: George Templeton Strong
eyes.role: 41-year-old Wall Street lawyer, Columbia College trustee, later treasurer of the U.S. Sanitary Commission
eyes.vantage_label: Northern city, far from the guns
eyes.authenticity: Daily diary of about four million words, 1835–1875, at the New-York Historical Society. Edited by Allan Nevins and Milton Halsey Thomas (4 vols, 1952); the Civil War volume was reissued in 1962.
eyes.bio: A conservative, sharp-eyed Manhattan patrician whose diary is the best running record of how the Northern establishment felt the war. He moved from contempt for 'abolitionists' to fierce Unionism and, by 1865, to grief for Lincoln.

sources.title: Last Best Hope of Earth: Strong diary, April 13–16, 1861
House Divided: Strong diary, 17 April 1861 (Nevins ed. 1962)
Green-Wood: 'The Union Forever'

eyes.name: Walt Whitman
eyes.role: Poet and journalist; from late 1862 a volunteer visitor in Washington army hospitals
eyes.where: Broadway, New York (1861); Washington hospitals (1863); Brooklyn (April 1865)
eyes.authenticity: 'Specimen Days' (1882) reworks his wartime notebooks and letters; some sections keep their original dates, others are recollections. The original notebooks survive (Library of Congress). Treat as notebook-based memoir, not a pure diary.
eyes.bio: Whitman heard Sumter's news on Broadway at midnight and spent the war's middle years nursing the wounded in Washington. His view is neither soldier's nor civilian's but the hospital ward's, and his writing on Lincoln's death became the nation's elegy.

eyes.name: Charlotte Forten (later Grimké)
eyes.role: 25-year-old free Black teacher from Philadelphia, sent by the Port Royal Relief Association
eyes.where: St. Helena Island and Camp Saxton, Port Royal, South Carolina
eyes.authenticity: Five manuscript journals (1854–1864, 1885–1892) at the Moorland-Spingarn Research Center, Howard University. Abridged ed. Ray Allen Billington (1953); full ed. Brenda Stevenson (1988).
eyes.bio: One of the few Black Northern teachers in the Port Royal experiment, she was both insider and outsider: freeborn and educated, teaching people just out of slavery. Her journal records Emancipation Day from among the dignitaries, at Colonel Higginson's table.

sources.title: Clements Library: 'This First Day of January'
Museum of the American Revolution: the journal
SC Sea Grant: 'Emancipation Day — The Freed People of Port Royal'

eyes.name: Thomas Wentworth Higginson
eyes.role: 39-year-old colonel, 1st South Carolina Volunteers (later 33rd USCT), the first Union regiment raised from formerly enslaved men
eyes.where: Camp Saxton, Smith plantation, near Beaufort SC
eyes.form: journal (dated camp diary within a later book)
eyes.authenticity: Dated camp journal published first as 'Leaves from an Officer's Journal' (Atlantic Monthly, 1864), then as chapter II of 'Army Life in a Black Regiment' (1870). Lightly edited for print but keeps its daily dates.
eyes.bio: A Unitarian minister, abolitionist and backer of John Brown, Higginson was a white officer who wrote with real (if often paternalist) attention to his men's songs, speech and courage. On 1 January 1863 he was the man holding the flag when the crowd began to sing.

sources.title: Army Life in a Black Regiment (Project Gutenberg)
House Divided: Emancipation among Black troops in South Carolina

eyes.name: Susie Baker King Taylor
eyes.role: 14-year-old who had escaped slavery in Savannah; laundress, nurse and teacher to the 1st SC Volunteers
eyes.where: Camp Saxton and the regiment's camps on the Sea Islands
eyes.authenticity: MEMOIR, not a diary: 'Reminiscences of My Life in Camp with the 33d United States Colored Troops' (Boston, 1902), written nearly 40 years later. The only published wartime account by a Black woman who served with a regiment. Dates are her recollection.
eyes.bio: Taylor gives the view from the camp itself: a teenage girl among soldiers she taught to read. Where Forten saw speeches, she remembered the barbecue and the joy. She is included because no wartime diary by a formerly enslaved person survives for this day.

sources.title: Documenting the American South: Reminiscences (1902)

eyes.name: Isaac W. K. Handy
eyes.where: Norfolk, Virginia (Union-occupied, exempted from the Proclamation)
eyes.vantage_label: hostile onlooker in an occupied city
eyes.authenticity: Manuscript diary in the Handy Family Papers, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan; pages digitised in the Clements exhibit. Handy was later held as a political prisoner at Fort Delaware.
eyes.bio: Handy watched Black Norfolk celebrate freedom in a city the Proclamation had pointedly left out. His hostile but detailed entry proves how far the news ran ahead of the law.

sources.title: Clements Library: Handy diary pages

eyes.name: Emilie Frances Davis
eyes.role: Free Black dressmaker and domestic worker in her twenties
eyes.authenticity: Three pocket diaries, 1863–1865, at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania; edited by Judith Giesberg as 'Emilie Davis's Civil War' (2014). Entries are very short. NOT RE-VERIFIED in this session: dates and content here rely on prior knowledge of the edition and are marked approx.
eyes.bio: Davis's terse daily notes (church, sewing, friends, letters from a sweetheart in the army) are rare: an ordinary free Black woman's war, day by day. She marks the great days in a few words, between errands.

eyes.name: Arthur James Lyon Fremantle
eyes.role: 28-year-old lieutenant-colonel, Coldstream Guards, on leave as a private observer
eyes.authenticity: Travel diary, April–July 1863, partly published in Blackwood's Magazine and as 'Three Months in the Southern States' (Edinburgh/London 1863; New York and Mobile reprints 1864). Dated entries, lightly edited for print; strongly sympathetic to the South.
eyes.bio: Fremantle crossed the Confederacy from Texas to Pennsylvania and reached Lee's army days before Gettysburg. His dated entries are the most-quoted eyewitness record of Lee and Longstreet on 2–3 July, and they later became a source for Shaara's 'The Killer Angels'.

sources.title: Three Months in the Southern States (Project Gutenberg)
Library of America Story of the Week: Fremantle at Gettysburg
HistoryNet review (Peter S. Carmichael)

eyes.name: Elisha Hunt Rhodes
eyes.role: Enlisted as a private in 1861 at 19; by 1863 a lieutenant, 2nd Rhode Island Infantry; colonel by 1865
eyes.side: Union (Army of the Potomac, VI Corps)
eyes.authenticity: Wartime diary, partly recopied by Rhodes after the war (one 1885 footnote shows later revision). Edited by his great-grandson Robert Hunt Rhodes as 'All for the Union' (1985); it was the voice of Ken Burns's 'The Civil War'. Gettysburg and Lincoln entries located via the edition index (pp. 114ff, 230–31); exact day-wording not re-checked.
eyes.bio: Rhodes served from Bull Run to Appomattox, rising from private to colonel, and wrote steadily throughout. His is the steady, pious, unglamorous voice of a Northern volunteer for whom the Union was the whole point.

sources.title: W. W. Norton: Rhodes diary excerpts, 1862
All for the Union index (Univ. of Alabama repository)

eyes.name: Gideon Welles
eyes.where: Washington: White House, Navy Department, the Petersen house
eyes.authenticity: Diary 1862–1869, Library of Congress. The 1911 three-volume edition includes some later revisions by Welles; the Welles diary edited by Howard K. Beale (1960) marks them. Core entries are contemporary.
eyes.bio: Welles, 'Father Neptune' to Lincoln, wrote one of the closest records of the wartime cabinet. He sat in a chair beside the dying President through the night of 14–15 April and noticed what others left out: the Black Washingtonians weeping in the rain.

sources.title: Britannica primary source: Welles on the death of Lincoln
Iron Brigader: Welles on Lincoln's death (from Diary vol. II)

eyes.name: Emma Florence LeConte
eyes.role: 17-year-old daughter of Joseph LeConte, chemistry professor at South Carolina College
eyes.where: LeConte house on the South Carolina College campus (then a hospital), Columbia
eyes.authenticity: Manuscript diary (31 Dec 1864 – Aug 1865) in the Southern Historical Collection, UNC-Chapel Hill; transcription on Documenting the American South. Published as 'When the World Ended' (1957).
eyes.bio: A bookish, furious teenager, LeConte watched Sherman's army enter Columbia and the city burn around the college. Her diary is the classic Confederate civilian account of 17 February 1865, written within hours, raw with hatred and fear.

sources.title: Documenting the American South: Emma LeConte diary summary
UNC '150 Years Ago Today' blog: LeConte excerpts

eyes.name: Sarah Katherine 'Kate' Stone
eyes.role: 20-year-old daughter of a widowed planter; Brokenburn plantation held about 150 enslaved people
eyes.where: Brokenburn, Madison Parish, Louisiana (30 miles NW of Vicksburg); refugee in Tyler, Texas, from late 1863
eyes.vantage_label: near the Vicksburg front, then a refugee
eyes.authenticity: Journal 1861–1868, edited by John Q. Anderson as 'Brokenburn: The Journal of Kate Stone' (LSU Press, 1955). Stone added a short retrospective introduction around 1900; the dated entries are wartime.
eyes.bio: Stone's journal tracks a Louisiana planter family's collapse as Grant's Vicksburg campaign floods and occupies their land. She fled to Texas with the enslaved people her family still held, and her reaction to Lincoln's murder shows how bitter Confederate civilians remained.

sources.title: Essential Civil War Curriculum: Kate Stone
House Divided: Kate Stone

eyes.name: John Beauchamp Jones
eyes.role: Novelist turned clerk in the Confederate War Department, aged about 51 in 1861
eyes.authenticity: Published as 'A Rebel War Clerk's Diary at the Confederate States Capital' (2 vols, Philadelphia, 1866), the year of his death; some passages were likely smoothed for print. NOT RE-VERIFIED in this session: entries are approx from prior knowledge.
eyes.bio: Jones sat at the paper-heavy centre of the Confederate war effort and recorded prices, rumours, hunger and gossip about Davis's cabinet. His diary shows the Southern capital learning of distant disasters by telegraph.

entries.headline: Woken by guns, she prays, then climbs to the roof
entries.digest: Her husband came back from Sumter with Anderson's refusal and went out again with the final terms. At about 4:30 a.m. the first gun sounded; she knelt and prayed as never before, then went up to the housetop with the other women to watch the shells burst over the harbour. A bystander called it a waste of ammunition, and by the end of the day she noted with relief that nobody had been hurt.
entries.source_note: Woodward ed. (1981), as excerpted by American Battlefield Trust and Emerging Civil War; 1880s revised text

entries.headline: Bombardment news electrifies the first Confederate capital
entries.digest: Jones had come south to seek a government post and was in Montgomery when the telegraph brought news of the bombardment. He recorded crowds, cheering, and his conviction that a great nation had been born. This is the start of a diary he kept until Richmond fell.
entries.source_note: A Rebel War Clerk's Diary (1866), opening entries; not re-verified this session

entries.headline: Sumter burns; the enslaved servants show nothing
entries.digest: Aides brought word that the fort was on fire and none of the Confederate guns had been silenced. Regular meals stopped because of the constant cannonade. What unsettled her most was the enslaved household staff, who went about their work with no visible reaction, and she wondered whether that calm meant indifference or something they were hiding until their time came.
entries.source_note: Woodward ed. (1981); HistoryNet 'Gossip flies as Sumter burns'

entries.headline: 'Civil War is inaugurated at last'
entries.digest: With Sumter's fall confirmed, Strong recorded that the city's mood was hardening fast. Men who had defended 'Southern rights' a week earlier now pledged themselves to the government, and even half-disloyal newspapers were turning. He noted that the change was not instant or universal, but it was pronounced.
entries.source_note: Last Best Hope of Earth transcription, Nevins ed.

entries.headline: Newsboys' extras under the lamps at midnight
entries.digest: Walking down Broadway late after the opera, Whitman heard newsboys running up the street shouting the attack on Sumter. He bought an extra and stood with a small crowd reading it under the hotel lamps; no one said much. He later made the moment the opening scene of his war.
entries.source_note: Specimen Days (1882), 'Opening of the Secession War'; recollection, not a contemporary entry

entries.headline: Raw recruits on Governor's Island
entries.digest: On the day Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers, Strong went to see about three hundred new recruits, most of them very raw. One farm boy told him he had enlisted to fight for Lincoln and expected hard knocks. Strong sensed the North drawing together and thought every man would be needed before the game was won or lost.
entries.source_note: Last Best Hope of Earth; Green-Wood 'The Union Forever'

entries.headline: The Herald converts; 'God save the Union'
entries.digest: Strong noted with satisfaction that the New York Herald, long friendly to the South, had completely changed sides. He recorded Burnside leaving his railroad post to lead Rhode Island volunteers and Massachusetts men crowding Faneuil Hall. He ended the entry with a prayer in capital letters for the Union and the confusion of its enemies.
entries.source_note: Green-Wood 'The Union Forever'; Last Best Hope of Earth

entries.headline: Flags everywhere in Manhattan
entries.digest: Strong's next entry continues the account of a city suddenly full of flags and war talk, with merchants who had traded with the South now speaking of loyalty. It is the third consecutive day on which a conservative lawyer records how quickly his class changed its mind.
entries.source_note: House Divided record, Nevins ed. (1962), pp. 122–123; content summarised, not re-read

entries.headline: Union lines hold at Malvern Hill
entries.digest: A year before Gettysburg, Rhodes recorded the last of the Seven Days battles: the Union line held and the Confederates fell back. Two days later he described a rainy night march to Harrison's Landing, exhausted and shelled in his sleep. The entries give the ordinary grind behind the famous dates.
entries.source_note: W. W. Norton excerpts of All for the Union (1862 entries)

entries.headline: Planning a barbecue for freedom
entries.digest: Two days before the Proclamation took effect, Higginson was organising a feast: oxen to roast whole, molasses and water, and new colours promised by friends in New York. The camp diary in the days before shows him worried about his men's coughs, amused by their sense of humour, and aware that the coming day was theirs.
entries.source_note: Army Life in a Black Regiment, ch. II, entries of 29–31 Dec 1862

entries.headline: A crowd sings 'My Country, 'tis of thee' unbidden
entries.digest: Freedpeople arrived by land and by steamer from about ten o'clock. After the chaplain's prayer, Dr. W. H. Brisbane read the Proclamation and Rev. Mansfield French presented the colours. As Higginson waved the flag, a few voices near the platform, an elderly man and two women, began 'My Country, 'tis of thee', and others joined. He motioned the white people on the platform to stay silent and let them finish. Then the color sergeants spoke and the men ate roast beef.
entries.quote: the choked voice of a race at last unloosed
entries.source_note: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/6764 , ch. II, 'January 1, 1863 (evening)'

entries.headline: 'The most glorious day this nation has yet seen'
entries.digest: Forten crossed on the steamer Flora with other teachers and was shown around the camp by the regiment's surgeon, Dr. Seth Rogers. From among the dignitaries she watched the Proclamation read and cheered, and judged the speeches by the Black color sergeants Prince Rivers and Robert Sutton very good. She dined at Higginson's table rather than on the soldiers' roast oxen, and saw how moved the colonel was.
entries.quote: The most glorious day this nation has yet seen
entries.source_note: Billington ed.; quoted in Clements Library exhibit, SC Sea Grant, UNC Press blog

entries.headline: A barbecue remembered forty years on
entries.digest: Taylor, then about fourteen, recalled the reading of the Proclamation and above all the feast that followed, with whole oxen roasted for the soldiers and guests. Where Forten wrote of speeches and dinner with officers, she remembered the crowd's joy. She was writing as a widow in Boston, decades later.
entries.quote: a glorious day for us all
entries.source_note: Reminiscences (1902), cited in Clements Library exhibit; memoir

entries.headline: A freedom procession in a city the Proclamation excluded
entries.digest: Handy watched a huge procession of Black men, women and children move through Norfolk with banners, sashes and the U.S. flag. He estimated it at somewhere between 3,000 and 15,000 people. They gave three cheers each for the flag, Lincoln and Liberty and ended at General Viele's house for a speech. Norfolk was exempt from the Proclamation, and Handy disapproved, but his entry records that the marchers believed their jubilee had come anyway.
entries.source_note: Handy Family Papers, Clements Library; digitised pages in the 'This First Day of January' exhibit

entries.headline: Watch-night and jubilee at church
entries.digest: Davis's first pocket-diary entry of the year marks the day the Proclamation took effect with a few words about church gatherings and celebration among Philadelphia's Black community. Then, as always, she moves on to visits and sewing.
entries.source_note: Giesberg ed., Emilie Davis's Civil War (2014); not re-verified this session

entries.headline: Packing the journal to flee Grant's army
entries.digest: With Union troops closing in on the parishes above Vicksburg, the Stone household prepared to run. Kate hid her journal in a packing box. Over the following weeks the levees were cut, the land flooded, and the people her family held as slaves began to leave or take things. The family fled in early April.
entries.source_note: Essential Civil War Curriculum summary of Brokenburn (Anderson ed.)

entries.headline: Up a tree for the first day's fight
entries.digest: Fremantle left camp at noon after Hill's corps had passed toward Gettysburg. He climbed a tree in the most commanding spot he could find and, from there, got a fair general idea of the Union position on the hills beyond the town. He was a spectator, delighted to be there.
entries.quote: climbed up a tree in the most commanding place
entries.source_note: Three Months in the Southern States; Library of America Story of the Week excerpt

entries.headline: Generals whittling sticks before the attack
entries.digest: In the morning he looked down on Lee, Hill, Longstreet and Hood in conference; Longstreet and Hood sat whittling sticks. Longstreet told him to go back to his tree for a view of the afternoon assault. Hood later remembered the Englishman wedged in the forks of a tree.
entries.source_note: Library of America excerpt of the 2 July entry

entries.headline: An all-night march, then the battle
entries.digest: The VI Corps marched through the night of 1–2 July from Manchester, Maryland, and the 2nd Rhode Island reached the field on the afternoon of 2 July, worn out, and was put into the line on the Union left. Rhodes recorded the dead and wounded around him and, by the 4th, the enemy's withdrawal in the rain. His tone is relief and gratitude to God rather than glory.
entries.source_note: All for the Union, pp. 114–117 (index); day-by-day wording not re-checked

entries.headline: 'I wouldn't have missed this for anything'
entries.digest: Arriving as Pickett's charge was breaking up, Fremantle told Longstreet he would not have missed it for anything; Longstreet replied with grim humour that he would have liked to miss it. Fremantle then watched Lee ride among the broken men coming back, telling them it was all his fault and they must rally. He saw Lee mildly rebuke an officer for beating his horse. Fremantle admired Lee's calm, but the scene he recorded is a defeat.
entries.quote: I wouldn't have missed this for anything
entries.source_note: https://gutenberg.org/files/20928/20928-h/20928-h.htm (entry for 3 July); passage not re-fetched this session

entries.headline: Longstreet explains what went wrong
entries.digest: In heavy rain the army began to fall back. Longstreet talked to Fremantle about the battle, putting the failure down to not concentrating enough troops for the attack on 2 July rather than to the idea of attacking at all. Fremantle decided to leave the army and make for the North.
entries.source_note: HistoryNet review (Carmichael) on the 4 July conversation

entries.headline: Bulletins of Meade's victory on Independence Day
entries.digest: In Washington, Whitman noted the holiday procession and a bulletin from Meade announcing the repulse of Lee. In the same weeks he describes the hospitals filling with Gettysburg wounded. Vicksburg's surrender came the same day, though news of it took days to arrive.
entries.source_note: Specimen Days (1882), entries for early July 1863; not re-verified this session

entries.headline: Welles carries the Vicksburg news to Lincoln
entries.digest: A dispatch from Admiral Porter told Welles that Vicksburg had surrendered on 4 July. He hurried to the White House, where Lincoln, overjoyed, said this would end the war in the West. Coming three days after Gettysburg, it was the best news the administration had had.
entries.source_note: Diary of Gideon Welles, vol. I, July 1863; not re-verified this session

entries.headline: Rumours of victory, then Vicksburg's fall
entries.digest: Richmond first heard reports that Lee had won in Pennsylvania. Within days came confirmation that Vicksburg had surrendered and that Lee was retreating. Jones recorded the gloom and rising prices in the War Department and the city.
entries.source_note: A Rebel War Clerk's Diary (1866), July 1863; not re-verified this session

entries.headline: The draft riots: Strong walks into the mob
entries.digest: As the first draft lottery set off riots, Strong went to see for himself. He described crowds attacking Black New Yorkers and buildings in flames, including the Colored Orphan Asylum, and he wrote with fury about the mainly Irish rioters and an almost absent city government. Ten days after Gettysburg, the war had reached Manhattan's streets.
entries.source_note: Nevins & Thomas ed., July 1863; not re-verified this session

entries.headline: Rumours, alarm and enlistments after Gettysburg
entries.digest: Lee's invasion threw Philadelphia into alarm, and Davis's short entries note the excitement, men going off, and the news of the battle. Black Philadelphians soon began enlisting at Camp William Penn.
entries.source_note: Giesberg ed. (2014); not re-verified this session

entries.place: LeConte house, South Carolina College, Columbia
entries.headline: The first close sight of the enemy
entries.digest: About one o'clock she heard shouting as Union troops came in. A guard was posted for the hospital on campus, and soldiers cooked dinner beside a board shelter at the gate. It was her first close look at Yankee soldiers other than as prisoners, and she felt only horror and hatred. Word came that Sherman had promised the mayor that private property would be safe.
entries.source_note: Diary as transcribed by Women History Blog and UNC '150 Years Ago Today'

entries.date_display: Saturday 18 February 1865 (recalling the night of the 17th)
entries.headline: The town 'wrapped in one huge blaze'
entries.digest: From the back piazza around seven she saw fires along the southern sky, then Hampton's house burning and a house on Sumter Street near enough to feel the heat. From the upper windows she watched soldiers fire homes, some using turpentine, while the guards joined in. College buildings caught fire while doctors fought from the roofs; wounded men crawled out. By morning she felt dull apathy and could not eat, furious that the family had believed Sherman's word.
entries.source_note: Women History Blog summary; UNC blog post of 18 Feb 2015

entries.headline: Refugee hears that Columbia is ashes
entries.digest: Having fled Columbia ahead of Sherman, Chesnut learned as a refugee in North Carolina that the city where she had lived was burned. In her later revision this is a time of rumour, bad food and grief among displaced Confederate women.
entries.source_note: Woodward ed. (1981), Feb 1865; 1880s revision; not re-verified this session

entries.headline: Columbia's fall and Charleston's evacuation reach Richmond
entries.digest: Jones recorded the news that Sherman had taken Columbia and that Charleston, where the war began, had been abandoned. Prices kept rising and he tallied his family's hunger.
entries.source_note: A Rebel War Clerk's Diary (1866), Feb 1865; not re-verified this session

entries.headline: Walking through the ruins
entries.digest: After the army left she walked into town and found it worse than she had imagined, literally in ruins, with chimneys standing over ash. She had already written that she believed no house in Columbia had escaped plunder, and that the family was living on a little corn, musty flour and bacon given by the enslaved household.
entries.source_note: UNC '150 Years Ago Today' posts of 21–22 Feb 2015

entries.headline: Richmond told to evacuate
entries.digest: The government received Lee's warning that the Petersburg lines had broken, and Davis left church to order the evacuation. Jones recorded the panic, the departing trains and his decision to stay with his family as the Confederacy collapsed around him.
entries.source_note: A Rebel War Clerk's Diary (1866), final entries; not re-verified this session

entries.place: Washington, Seward's house and the Petersen house
entries.headline: Called from bed to a dying President
entries.digest: A messenger woke Welles with news that Lincoln and Seward had been attacked. He went first to Seward's house and then with Stanton to the house across from Ford's Theatre. A doctor told him the President was effectively dead but might live some hours. Welles went in a little after eleven and later took a vacant chair beside the bed, where he sat for nearly two hours.
entries.source_note: Diary of Gideon Welles vol. II; Britannica and Iron Brigader transcriptions

entries.headline: 7:22 a.m., then the weeping in the rain
entries.digest: Rain began about six; Welles stepped out briefly, feeling faint. Lincoln died at twenty-two minutes past seven, Robert Lincoln broke down, and Dr. Gurley prayed. The cabinet signed a letter informing Andrew Johnson the government had passed to him. Outside the White House Welles saw several hundred Black Washingtonians, mostly women and children, overwhelmed with grief, and Tad asked who had killed his father.
entries.source_note: Diary of Gideon Welles vol. II; Britannica primary source

entries.headline: Wall Street goes silent
entries.digest: News of the assassination brought business in New York to a halt, and Strong described crowds, black drapery going up, and grief turning to anger. He wrote that the man he had once doubted had grown into a great President.
entries.source_note: Nevins & Thomas ed., April 1865; not re-verified this session

entries.headline: Very sad news of the President
entries.digest: Davis's entry records the news of Lincoln's death and the gloom it cast over the city. In the following days she notes the mourning and, later, Lincoln's body lying in state at Independence Hall.
entries.source_note: Giesberg ed. (2014); not re-verified this session

entries.headline: From victory to mourning in a week
entries.digest: Days after celebrating Lee's surrender, Rhodes's regiment heard that Lincoln had been murdered. He recorded the army's grief and anger and the sense that victory had suddenly gone sour.
entries.source_note: All for the Union, pp. 230–31 (index entry 'Lincoln assassination')

entries.headline: A note on 'the greatest, best' personality
entries.digest: Whitman was at home with his mother when the news came. The family could not eat, and they passed the papers silently between them. In his notes dated the 16th he called Lincoln the most dramatic and most characteristic figure in American history so far. The grief became 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd'.
entries.source_note: Specimen Days (1882), 'Death of President Lincoln'; later recollection plus dated note

entries.headline: Lincoln dead, and the South blamed for it
entries.digest: Chesnut heard the rumour, then the confirmation, that Lincoln had been killed. In her later version she foresaw that the murder would bring harsher treatment for the defeated South rather than relief.
entries.source_note: Woodward ed. (1981), April 1865; 1880s revision; not re-verified this session

entries.headline: A refugee cheers the assassin
entries.digest: Far from the war's end in Virginia, Stone wrote with open satisfaction at Lincoln's death and praised John Wilkes Booth. Reliable news of Lee's surrender had not yet arrived, so she still hoped the Confederacy might fight on. By mid-May she would be writing in despair.
entries.source_note: House Divided lists the 28 April 1865 entry; Essential Civil War Curriculum summarises her reaction

convergences.label: Bombardment and fall of Fort Sumter (12–13 April 1861)
convergences.note: Chesnut watches from a Charleston rooftop with her husband part of the plot. A day later Strong in Manhattan and Whitman on Broadway read the same news as a call to arms, and Jones in Montgomery reads it as a nation's birth. The same news reached four cities, and each read it differently.

convergences.label: Emancipation Proclamation takes effect; Camp Saxton celebration
convergences.note: Three people stood within yards of each other at Camp Saxton: the white colonel holding the flag, the free Black teacher on the platform, and the formerly enslaved teenager in the crowd. Higginson heard the singing, Forten the speeches, Taylor remembered the feast. In Norfolk a hostile minister recorded a vast procession in a city the Proclamation excluded, and in Philadelphia Davis marked the day between errands. The surgeon Seth Rogers (letter of 1 Jan), teacher Harriet Ware (letter) and Laura Towne (diary, who missed the ferry) add further eyes on the same platform.

convergences.label: Gettysburg and Vicksburg (1–4 July 1863)
convergences.note: Fremantle watched from Lee's side of the field while Rhodes, after an all-night march, stood in the Union line facing him. Whitman nursed the wounded as they came to Washington, and Welles brought Lincoln the Vicksburg news. Jones heard the rumours sour in Richmond. Ten days later Strong watched New York tear itself apart over the draft.

convergences.label: Sherman's army enters Columbia; the city burns
convergences.note: LeConte wrote from inside the fire, within hours; Chesnut and Jones only heard of it, from exile and from Richmond. The reader should weigh LeConte's raw testimony against the later dispute over whether retreating Confederates, drunken soldiers or deliberate orders started the fires.

convergences.label: Lincoln shot (14 April) and dies (7:22 a.m., 15 April)
convergences.note: Welles watched him die, and the news then spread across the country: to Wall Street, to Black Philadelphia, to a regiment in Virginia, and to Whitman's breakfast table. Two weeks later in Texas, Kate Stone cheered the assassin. No single day in this chapter divides its diarists more sharply.

ties.note: Forten dined at Higginson's table on Emancipation Day and later wrote an Atlantic article on the Sea Islands; both published in the Atlantic Monthly in 1864.
Taylor served for years with Higginson's regiment; he wrote a short letter supporting her 1902 Reminiscences.

Both were teaching freedpeople in the Port Royal district in 1863. One was freeborn in Philadelphia and the other had escaped slavery in Savannah, and they recorded the same ceremony from opposite ends of the crowd.
On 2–3 July 1863 the British observer sat with Longstreet's staff while Rhodes's VI Corps held the Union line opposite.
Both lived in Columbia during the war; Chesnut fled shortly before Sherman arrived, and LeConte stayed to watch it burn.
They held two ends of Union power: Welles inside the cabinet, Strong in New York's establishment, whose Sanitary Commission work often took him to Washington. Both wrote about 15 April 1865.
Fremantle crossed the Trans-Mississippi from Texas through Louisiana in spring 1863, the same refugee roads the Stone family used weeks earlier.
Both wrote about Jefferson Davis's Richmond circle: Chesnut from its drawing rooms and Jones from its clerks' desks.
Whitman watched Lincoln ride through Washington's streets in 1863–64; Welles sat beside his deathbed. Both made his death the centre of their record.

threads_out.note: Higginson and Forten grew up in an abolitionism shaped by the Haitian Revolution, the revolutionary offshoot of 1789. The Emancipation Day rhetoric of liberty and jubilee echoes the Rights of Man.

Tsar Alexander II freed Russia's serfs in 1861, the same spring as Fort Sumter. Russia's fleets visited New York and San Francisco in 1863, and Strong and Welles both wrote about the visit as a gesture of friendship.
The Civil War's industrial killing (rifled guns, railways, trenches at Petersburg) foreshadowed 1914–18. European observers like Fremantle mostly missed that lesson.
Juneteenth, the Black regiments and the long fight over how the war is remembered (the Lost Cause in Chesnut and Stone versus freedom in Forten and Taylor) carry on long after 1865.
The Union's demand for unconditional surrender, coined by Grant at Fort Donelson in 1862, became Allied policy at Casablanca in 1943.
